EnergyPulse AI — Machine Learning Notebook¶

Evaluation 2: trained and evaluated models¶

Goal. Forecast the expected electricity consumption of a meter for the next 24 hours, then flag readings that deviate from what was expected so that a person can review them.

Rubric item Where it is answered
Dataset quality and justification Section 1
Proper preprocessing with no data leakage Sections 1, 3, 4 and 5
Model choice with at least one baseline Sections 6 and 7
Evaluation metrics and interpretation Sections 8, 9, 10 and 11

Everything is real data: no synthetic or AI-generated dataset is used for training. All numbers printed below are produced by running this notebook.

The reusable code lives in ml/src/ (the notebook imports it, so the notebook and the scripts can never disagree): config.py → settings, prepare_data.py → cleaning, features.py → features, train_forecast.py → models, anomaly.py → anomaly detection.

1. Dataset¶

Source. ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014, UCI Machine Learning Repository — https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/321/electricityloaddiagrams20112014

Property Value
What it is Real smart-meter readings of 370 clients in Portugal
Size 140,256 rows × 370 meters (one reading every 15 minutes, 2011–2014)
Unit average kW in each 15-minute interval → kWh = kW ÷ 4
Missing values none in the file (but zeros before a meter was connected)
Labels none — nobody marked which readings are faults

Why this dataset fits the project

  • It is real measured data from a public, citable source (not generated).
  • It has the same shape as the app's input: a meter's history of interval readings (what the user uploads as CSV).
  • Four years at 15-minute resolution contain every pattern we need to learn: day/night, weekday/weekend, summer/winter, holidays.
  • 370 different clients let us test on small and large consumers, and on meters the model has never seen.

Known limitations (stated up front)

  • No anomaly labels → we can measure the forecast error exactly, but anomaly detection can only be evaluated indirectly (Sections 10–11).
  • No weather data and no description of each client (home, shop, factory).
  • One country, 2011–2014.

1.1 Cleaning — done once by ml/src/prepare_data.py¶

The raw file is 711 MB, so the cleaning runs as a script and saves a small hourly file that this notebook loads. Steps:

  1. Read the file (; separator, decimal comma).
  2. Daylight-saving repair (two artefacts per year, verified on the raw rows) — code below.
  3. Convert kW → kWh and aggregate 4 quarter-hours into 1 hourly value. Hourly data is less noisy and matches the day-ahead task.
  4. Keep 2012–2014 only: in 2011, 211 of 370 meters are mostly zeros because they were not connected yet.
  5. Keep eligible meters: at most 0.5 % zero readings and no outage longer than 3 hours.
  6. Pick 20 meters to model and 10 extra meters that are never used for training, by a stratified random draw over consumption level (fixed seed).
In [2]:
show(P.fix_daylight_saving)

def fix_daylight_saving(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Repair the two daylight-saving artefacts (verified on the raw file).

    Last Sunday of March - the clock jumps from 01:00 to 02:00, so the local
        hour 01:00-01:59 does not exist. The file still has 4 rows for it
        (01:00, 01:15, 01:30, 01:45) holding zeros or tiny placeholder values.
        They are not real consumption -> mark them as missing (NaN).
    Last Sunday of October - the hour 01:00-01:59 happens twice and the file
        stores the SUM of both -> divide the 4 rows by 2.
    """
    df = df.copy()
    for year in sorted(set(df.index.year)):
        for month in (3, 10):
            day = last_sunday(year, month)
            mask = (df.index >= day + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)) & (df.index < day + pd.Timedelta(hours=2))
            if mask.any():
                df.loc[mask] = np.nan if month == 3 else df.loc[mask] / 2
    return df

1.2 What the data looks like¶

Patterns are checked on the training period only, so nothing we learn here comes from validation or test.

In [4]:
m = C.SHOWCASE_METER
PL.save(PL.seasonality(hourly.loc[:C.TRAIN_END, m], m), "01_seasonality");

Reading the figure (example meter). There is a strong daily cycle: about 90 kWh per hour at night and about 190 kWh during the day. This meter runs seven days a week, so its weekday and weekend profiles are almost the same — other meters in the sample do drop at weekends, which is why the day of the week is still a feature. Over the year the level changes mildly and peaks in late summer. Daily, weekly and yearly seasonality are what the features in Section 3 describe (hour, day of week, month, and the values 24 h and 168 h earlier).

2. The forecasting task¶

At any hour t, predict the consumption of hour t using only information that existed 24 hours earlier.

This is a day-ahead forecast: it matches the dashboard card "forecast horizon: next 24 hours".

It is also the right design for anomaly detection: if the model could see the last hour, a spike would immediately raise the next "expected" value and hide a problem that lasts several hours. With a 24-hour gap, the expected value stays clean.

3. Feature engineering (no leakage)¶

Group Features Meaning
Lagged demand lag_24, lag_48, lag_72, lag_168, lag_336 same hour 1, 2, 3 days ago and 1, 2 weeks ago
Rolling statistics roll_mean_24, roll_std_24, roll_min_24, roll_max_24, roll_std_168 level and variability of the most recent day/week we are allowed to see
Typical hour same_hour_mean_4w average of this exact hour-of-week in the previous 4 weeks
Calendar hour, dayofweek, is_weekend, month, is_holiday seasonality; known in advance (Portuguese public holidays)

Leakage rule: every lag is ≥ 24 h and every rolling window is computed on the series shifted by 24 h.

In [5]:
show(F.build_features)

def build_features(y: pd.Series) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One meter -> table with target, scale and raw (kWh) features."""
    h = C.HORIZON
    df = pd.DataFrame({"y": y})

    # 1) lagged demand: same hour 1, 2, 3 days ago and 1, 2 weeks ago
    for lag in C.LAGS:
        df[f"lag_{lag}"] = y.shift(lag)

    # 2) rolling statistics of the most recent data we are allowed to see
    past = y.shift(h)                       # newest value inside every window is y[t-24]
    df["roll_mean_24"] = past.rolling(24).mean()
    df["roll_std_24"] = past.rolling(24).std()
    df["roll_min_24"] = past.rolling(24).min()
    df["roll_max_24"] = past.rolling(24).max()
    df["roll_mean_168"] = past.rolling(168).mean()
    df["roll_std_168"] = past.rolling(168).std()

    # 3) typical level of this exact hour-of-week (mean of the previous 4 weeks)
    df["same_hour_mean_4w"] = sum(y.shift(168 * k) for k in range(1, C.SAME_HOUR_WEEKS + 1)) / C.SAME_HOUR_WEEKS

    # 4) calendar / seasonality features - known in advance
    idx = df.index
    df["hour"] = idx.hour
    df["dayofweek"] = idx.dayofweek
    df["is_weekend"] = (idx.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int)
    df["month"] = idx.month
    holidays = portugal_holidays(range(idx.year.min(), idx.year.max() + 1))
    df["is_holiday"] = pd.Series(idx.date, index=idx).isin(holidays).astype(int)

    # 5) scale = the meter's average hourly consumption over the last visible week
    df["scale"] = df["roll_mean_168"].clip(lower=1e-6)
    df = df.drop(columns="roll_mean_168")

    return df.dropna()                      # first 4 weeks have no lag history

3.1 Automatic leakage test¶

If a feature secretly used recent data, changing that data would change the feature. So we corrupt everything after t − 24 h and check that the features of hour t stay identical. We repeat this for 200 random hours.

In [7]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = hourly[m]
cols = [c for c in feat.columns if c != "y"]
checked = 0
for t in rng.choice(feat.index[1000:], size=200, replace=False):
    t = pd.Timestamp(t)
    corrupted = y.copy()
    corrupted.loc[t - pd.Timedelta(hours=C.HORIZON - 1):] = rng.uniform(0, 1e6, size=len(corrupted.loc[t - pd.Timedelta(hours=C.HORIZON - 1):]))
    a = feat.loc[t, cols]
    b = F.build_features(corrupted).loc[t, cols]
    assert np.allclose(a.values.astype(float), b.values.astype(float)), f"LEAK at {t}"
    checked += 1
print(f"PASSED: {checked} random hours - no feature changes when the last 23 hours + the target hour are corrupted.")

PASSED: 200 random hours - no feature changes when the last 23 hours + the target hour are corrupted.

4. Scaling — one model for all meters¶

Meters differ by a factor of 400 in size. Instead of a global StandardScaler (which would have to be fitted on some data and could leak), each row is divided by a number computed from that meter's own past:

scale(t) = mean hourly kWh of the last visible week (t−191 h … t−24 h)

The target and every kWh feature are divided by scale, so a normal reading is around 1.0 for every meter. The model predicts the scaled value and we multiply back to get kWh.

Why this matters:

  • No leakage: the scale of a row only uses data older than 24 h — nothing is fitted on validation or test.
  • One shared model learns from 20 meters at once (more data than 20 separate models).
  • The model is scale-free, so it can be applied to a new meter uploaded by a user.
In [8]:
show(F.scale_table)

def scale_table(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Divide the target and all kWh features by `scale`.
    A 5 kWh shop and a 2,500 kWh factory become comparable (values around 1.0),
    so ONE model can learn from all meters and can serve a brand-new meter."""
    out = df.copy()
    for c in LEVEL_FEATURES:
        out[c] = out[c] / out["scale"]
    out["y_scaled"] = out["y"] / out["scale"]
    return out

5. Chronological split¶

Time-series data must never be shuffled: a random split would put future hours in the training set and let the model "predict" the past.

The test set is a full year, so the score covers all seasons and holidays.

6. Baselines¶

A model is only useful if it beats a simple rule. Two rules that need no training:

  • Seasonal Naive (weekly) — "same hour last week": ŷ(t) = y(t − 168). This is the baseline named in the proposal.
  • Seasonal Naive (daily) — "same hour yesterday": ŷ(t) = y(t − 24). On this data it is the stronger baseline, so we report it too and compare against the better of the two — beating only the weak one would be misleading.

Both respect the 24-hour rule.

7. Models and tuning¶

Model Why
Random Forest robust, few settings, handles non-linear interactions (hour × weekday) without scaling
XGBoost gradient boosting; usually the strongest model on tabular features; small and fast to serve

Each configuration is fitted on train and scored on validation. For XGBoost, early stopping also watches validation only. The test year is not touched in this section.

8. Results¶

Metrics

  • MAE (kWh) — average size of the error; easy to read.
  • RMSE (kWh) — like MAE but punishes large errors more; important here because large misses are what create false alerts.
  • WAPE (%) = Σ|error| ÷ Σ|actual| — MAE as a share of consumption. It lets us compare a 6 kWh meter with a 2,500 kWh meter, and unlike MAPE it does not explode when one reading is near zero.

MAE and RMSE are in kWh, so they are reported per meter; WAPE is averaged across meters.

def versus_baselines(d):
    s = T.score_table(d)
    out = {}
    for metric in ["MAE", "RMSE", "WAPE"]:
        p = s.pivot(index="meter", columns="model", values=metric)
        best_base = p[["naive_weekly", "naive_daily"]].min(axis=1)
        out[metric] = {"meters where XGBoost beats BOTH baselines": f"{int((p.xgb < best_base).sum())} of {len(p)}",
                       "avg. reduction vs weekly naive": f"{(1 - p.xgb / p.naive_weekly).mean():.1%}",
                       "avg. reduction vs daily naive": f"{(1 - p.xgb / p.naive_daily).mean():.1%}"}
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

Random Forest 7.85% vs XGBoost 7.91% on test (validation: RF 8.02% vs XGBoost 7.97%).

Interpretation¶

  • The models beat both baselines on every modelled meter, on all three metrics. The gain is larger on RMSE than on MAE, which means the models mainly remove the large misses of the naive rules. That is expected: "same hour yesterday" is wrong whenever today is a different kind of day than yesterday, and "same hour last week" is wrong after any change of level.
  • Random Forest and XGBoost are practically tied. XGBoost was chosen because it was slightly better on validation (the only place where we are allowed to choose) and because it is a few MB and fast to serve, while a forest of this size is hundreds of MB. We do not switch to whichever model is ahead on the test set — that would be using the test set for model selection.
  • Validation and test errors are close, so the model did not overfit the tuning period.
  • Not every meter is predictable. A few meters have irregular behaviour (their level jumps between months); every method, including the baselines, has a high error there. On the 10 unseen meters the model is better for the regular ones but does not beat the baselines on all of them, and the mean is dominated by two irregular meters — the median tells the typical story. Consequence for the app: a new meter should get a "forecast quality" check before its alerts are trusted.
  • An error of about 8 % a day ahead, without weather data, is the noise floor that the anomaly detector must work above.

Reading the three figures

  • One week: the forecast follows the daily shape closely. The weekly naive line simply repeats last week, so it is off whenever this week differs from the previous one (visible on 14–16 May).
  • Error by hour / month: the model is better than both baselines at every hour and in every month. All methods are weakest in the months with the most holidays and weather-driven change.
  • Feature importance: the model relies mostly on "same hour yesterday" and "typical level of this hour in the last 4 weeks", then corrects with the other lags and the calendar. That is sensible behaviour, not a black box.

10. Anomaly detection¶

The forecast answers "what was expected?". An anomaly is a reading that is far from it.

Method A — forecast-residual thresholds (EnergyPulse method)¶

  1. residual = (actual − expected) ÷ scale
  2. From the validation residuals, learn for every meter and every hour of the day what a normal residual looks like: its median and its MAD (median absolute deviation). Night hours and working hours get their own tolerance — this is the context-aware part.
  3. On the test year compute the robust z-score z = 0.6745 × (residual − median) ÷ MAD and flag the hour when |z| > 3.5 (the standard modified z-score rule of Iglewicz & Hoaglin).
  4. Neighbouring flagged hours are merged into one alert with its excess kWh and estimated cost.

Median/MAD are used instead of mean/standard deviation because the anomalies themselves would inflate a standard deviation and hide each other.

Thresholds come from validation residuals that the model produced out-of-sample (the model that predicted them was trained on train only), and are then frozen before looking at 2014.

In [22]:
show(A.fit_thresholds); show(A.robust_z)

def fit_thresholds(val: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per meter and hour of day: median and MAD of the validation residuals."""
    r = val.assign(hour=val.index.hour)
    g = r.groupby(["meter", "hour"])["rel_resid"]
    med = g.median().rename("median")
    mad = g.apply(lambda s: (s - s.median()).abs().median()).rename("mad")
    return pd.concat([med, mad], axis=1).reset_index()

def robust_z(df: pd.DataFrame, thr: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Modified z-score: 0.6745 * (x - median) / MAD  (robust to outliers)."""
    key = pd.DataFrame({"meter": df["meter"].values, "hour": df.index.hour})
    t = key.merge(thr, on=["meter", "hour"], how="left")
    return 0.6745 * (df["rel_resid"].values - t["median"].values) / t["mad"].clip(lower=1e-9).values
In [23]:
val_a, test_a = A.add_residuals(val), A.add_residuals(test)
thr = A.fit_thresholds(val_a)
val_a["z"], test_a["z"] = A.robust_z(val_a, thr), A.robust_z(test_a, thr)
val_a["flag_resid"] = val_a.z.abs() > C.ROBUST_Z_THRESHOLD
test_a["flag_resid"] = test_a.z.abs() > C.ROBUST_Z_THRESHOLD
print(f"flagged hours - validation: {val_a.flag_resid.mean():.2%}   test: {test_a.flag_resid.mean():.2%}")
PL.save(PL.z_timeline(test_a[test_a.meter == m], m), "09_z_timeline");

This is the "reviewable case" of the proposal, now produced by the trained model: the alert shows when it started, what was expected, how much energy was above expectation and what that costs at the user's tariff. It is a deviation to review, not a proven fault.

Method B — Isolation Forest (comparison)¶

An unsupervised model that isolates unusual points with random splits. It gets a scale-free description of each reading without the forecast: the reading itself, its difference from yesterday / last week / the 4-week typical value, the hour and the weekend flag. It is fitted on train; its alert budget is set on validation to the same share of flagged hours as Method A, so the comparison is fair.

In [26]:
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
iforest = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, max_samples=2048, random_state=C.RANDOM_SEED, n_jobs=-1)
iforest.fit(A.if_table(train)[A.IF_FEATURES])
val_a["if_score"] = iforest.score_samples(A.if_table(val_a)[A.IF_FEATURES])
test_a["if_score"] = iforest.score_samples(A.if_table(test_a)[A.IF_FEATURES])
if_thr = {k: g.if_score.quantile(max(g.flag_resid.mean(), 1e-4)) for k, g in val_a.groupby("meter")}
test_a["flag_iforest"] = test_a.if_score < test_a.meter.map(if_thr)

both = (test_a.flag_resid & test_a.flag_iforest).sum()
either = (test_a.flag_resid | test_a.flag_iforest).sum()
pd.DataFrame({"test year": {
    "hours flagged by residual thresholds": f"{test_a.flag_resid.mean():.2%}",
    "hours flagged by Isolation Forest": f"{test_a.flag_iforest.mean():.2%}",
    "hours flagged by both": f"{both:,}",
    "overlap (Jaccard)": f"{both / either:.1%}",
    "flagged hours that fall on a public holiday": f"{test_a[test_a.flag_resid].is_holiday.mean():.1%}",
    "share of all hours that are public holidays": f"{test_a.is_holiday.mean():.1%}"}})

Reviewing the alerts (no labels → honest reading)¶

  • The share of flagged hours on validation and on test is nearly the same, so the frozen thresholds transfer to a new year.
  • The two methods agree on only a minority of hours: they look for different things. Isolation Forest flags readings that are rare in general; the residual method flags readings that are unexpected for this meter at this hour.
  • Public holidays are heavily over-represented among the alerts (Christmas, New Year, 8 December lead the list). These are real deviations from the normal pattern but they have an obvious explanation — exactly the kind of alert a user would mark as "Expected". This is the evidence for the human-in-the-loop review step, and it tells us the false-alert rate is not zero.
  • Alert volume differs a lot between meters: irregular meters produce many alerts. The sensitivity (the 3.5 threshold) is therefore a user setting in the app.

11. Controlled injection test¶

Because the data has no labels, we create a situation where the truth is known: we take the real test-year readings and multiply 3 consecutive hours by 1.2, 1.4, 1.7 or 2.0 at 30 random moments per meter (600 events per size). Then we rebuild the features, run both detectors and count how many injected events are caught.

  • This is an evaluation technique only. The models and thresholds were already frozen; nothing is trained on the injected values, and the dataset itself stays 100 % real.
  • A spike counts as detected if at least one of its 3 hours is flagged as above expected.
In [28]:
inj = A.injection_test(hourly, modelled, xgb_model, thr, iforest, if_thr, test_a)
PL.save(PL.injection(inj), "12_injection_test")
inj.rename(columns={"magnitude_pct": "spike size (%)", "recall_residual": "detected - residual (%)",
                    "recall_iforest": "detected - Isolation Forest (%)",
                    "alert_rate_other_hours_residual": "other hours flagged - residual (%)",
                    "alert_rate_other_hours_iforest": "other hours flagged - Isolation Forest (%)"})

spike size (%) events detected - residual (%) detected - Isolation Forest (%) other hours flagged - residual (%) other hours flagged - Isolation Forest (%)
0 20 600 57.17 30.00 2.01 3.35
1 40 600 87.17 69.83 1.98 3.68
2 70 600 96.50 89.50 1.95 4.42
3 100 600 98.67 94.50 1.93 4.76

Interpretation

  • The residual method catches more injected spikes than Isolation Forest at every size, while flagging fewer of the other hours. Knowing what was expected for this hour is what makes the difference.
  • Small spikes (+20 %) are caught only about half of the time: they are close to the normal forecast error (about 8 %, larger for some hours). Very small deviations cannot be separated from noise — a limitation we state rather than hide.
  • "Other hours flagged" is not a false-positive rate: those hours contain the real unusual events of 2014 (holidays, outages). It is the alert workload a user would see.
  • Injected spikes are simpler than real faults, so these percentages are an optimistic guide, not a guarantee.

13. Limitations and next steps¶

Limitation What we do about it
No anomaly labels alerts are "deviations to review"; user feedback (Expected / Investigate) will become the first labelled data
No weather data error is highest in seasons with weather-driven demand; temperature is the first feature to add
20 of 273 eligible meters modelled the selection is stratified and reproducible; the pipeline is the same for any number of meters
Irregular meters are hard for every method add a forecast-quality check when a new meter is uploaded
Holidays trigger alerts holiday flag is already a feature; the review step lets the user dismiss them
Small deviations (< 20 %) are often missed sensitivity is a user setting; longer events are easier to catch than short ones

Next evaluation: serve xgb_forecaster.json behind a FastAPI endpoint and connect it to the UI.
